title: The Human Eye and the Colourful World
subject: science
syllabus_note: Follows the CBSE 2025-26 syllabus: functioning of a lens in the human eye, defects of vision and their corrections, applications of spherical mirrors and lenses; refraction of light through a prism, dispersion of light, scattering of light, applications in daily life.

blocks.title: Why do stars twinkle but planets don't?
blocks.body:
Look at the night sky: the stars twinkle, but bright planets such as Jupiter shine steadily. The midday sky is blue, yet the setting Sun looks red, and to astronauts the sky is black.

Light, the eye and the air around us explain all of these. In this chapter you will learn how the eye focuses, how its common defects are corrected with lenses, how a prism splits white light into colours, and why the sky has the colours it has.

blocks.title: The scientist who explained the colour of the sea
blocks.body:
Chandrasekhara Venkata Raman wondered, on a voyage to Europe in 1921, why the sea is so deeply blue. His experiments on the **scattering of light** led, on 28 February 1928, to the discovery of the **Raman effect**: scattered light can change its colour slightly, revealing the molecules it met.

In 1930 he became the first Asian to win the **Nobel Prize in Physics**. India celebrates 28 February as **National Science Day**.
blocks.future: Optics and vision lead to careers in ophthalmology, optometry, physics research, meteorology, photography and the design of cameras and screens.

blocks.question: When you look from your book to a distant tree, what changes inside your eye so that both look sharp?
options: The distance of the retina from the lens
The focal length of the eye lens
blocks.explanation: The ciliary muscles change the curvature of the eye lens, and so its focal length: this is accommodation.

blocks.title: Parts of the eye and accommodation
blocks.body:
- **Cornea:** the clear front bulge; most of the refraction of light happens here.
- **Iris:** the coloured muscular diaphragm that controls the size of the **pupil**, and so the amount of light entering.
- **Eye lens:** a flexible, transparent, convex lens that fine-tunes the focus. It forms a **real, inverted** image on the **retina**.
- **Ciliary muscles:** hold the lens and change its curvature.
- **Retina:** a light-sensitive screen with cells that send electrical signals through the **optic nerve** to the brain, which interprets them.

**Power of accommodation:** the ability of the eye lens to adjust its focal length. For a far object the ciliary muscles relax and the lens becomes thin (longer focal length); for a near object they contract and the lens becomes thick (shorter focal length).

- **Near point:** the closest point seen clearly without strain, about **25 cm** for a young adult (the least distance of distinct vision).
- **Far point:** the farthest point seen clearly, **infinity** for a normal eye.

In old age, the lens can become milky and cloudy: this is **cataract**, treated by surgery.

blocks.question: The change in focal length of the eye lens is caused by the action of the:
blocks.explanation: The ciliary muscles change the curvature, and hence the focal length, of the eye lens.
option_feedback: The iris controls the pupil size.
The pupil only lets light in.

blocks.title: Myopia, hypermetropia and presbyopia
blocks.body:
- **Myopia (near-sightedness):** a person sees near objects clearly but not far ones. The image of a distant object forms **in front of** the retina. It is corrected with a **concave lens** of focal length equal to the far point (with a minus sign), which makes the parallel rays appear to come from the far point.
- **Hypermetropia (far-sightedness):** a person sees far objects clearly but not near ones; the near point is farther than 25 cm. The image of a near object forms **behind** the retina. It is corrected with a **convex lens**, which makes an object at 25 cm appear to be at the person's near point.
- **Presbyopia:** with age, the ciliary muscles weaken and the lens stiffens, so the near point moves away. Some people have both myopia and presbyopia and use **bifocal lenses**: concave in the upper part for distance, convex in the lower part for reading.

These defects can be corrected with spectacles, contact lenses or surgery.

blocks.title: Defects of vision at a glance
blocks.body:
| Defect | What goes wrong | Where the image forms | Causes | Correction |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Myopia (near-sightedness) | far objects look blurred; far point is nearer than infinity | in front of the retina | eye lens too curved; eyeball too long | concave lens |
| Hypermetropia (far-sightedness) | near objects look blurred; near point is farther than 25 cm | behind the retina | focal length of eye lens too long; eyeball too small | convex lens |
| Presbyopia | near objects blurred with age | behind the retina (for near objects) | ciliary muscles weaken and the eye lens becomes less flexible | convex lens, or bifocal lenses if both defects are present |

blocks.title: Worked example: correcting myopia
blocks.problem: The far point of a myopic person is 80 cm in front of the eye. Find the nature and power of the corrective lens.
steps: A concave lens must form an image of a distant object at the far point: $u = \infty$, $v = -80$ cm, so $f = -80$ cm $= -0.8$ m
blocks.answer: A concave lens of power −1.25 D.

blocks.question: A student cannot read the blackboard from the last row. The defect and its correction are:
blocks.explanation: Difficulty seeing far objects is myopia, corrected with a concave lens.
option_feedback: Presbyopia comes with age and affects near vision.
Cataract is a cloudy lens, treated by surgery.

sections.title: Refraction and dispersion by a prism

blocks.title: Splitting white light
blocks.body:
A glass **prism** has two inclined refracting surfaces; the angle between them is the **angle of the prism**. A ray passing through it bends twice, towards the base, and the angle between the incident and emergent rays is the **angle of deviation**.

**Dispersion:** white light entering a prism splits into a band of colours, the **spectrum**: **VIBGYOR** (violet, indigo, blue, green, yellow, orange, red). Different colours bend by different amounts because the speed of light in glass is different for each colour: **violet bends the most and red the least**.

Isaac Newton showed that a second, inverted prism recombines the colours into white light: white light is a mixture of seven colours.

**Rainbow:** a natural spectrum seen in the sky opposite the Sun after rain. Each water droplet acts like a small prism: sunlight is **refracted and dispersed** on entering, **reflected internally**, and **refracted** again on leaving.

blocks.question: In the spectrum formed by a prism, which colour bends the least?
blocks.explanation: Red light travels fastest in glass, so it bends the least; violet bends the most.

blocks.title: A moving, uneven atmosphere
blocks.body:
The air above a fire flickers because hot air is optically rarer than the cooler air around it, and the physical conditions keep changing. The whole atmosphere behaves like this on a large scale: its refractive index increases gradually towards the earth's surface. This **atmospheric refraction** explains:

- **Twinkling of stars:** a star is a point source far away. Its light bends as it passes through the atmosphere, so its apparent position is slightly higher than the real one; as the air moves, the position and the amount of light entering the eye keep changing, so the star twinkles.
- **Planets do not twinkle:** they are much nearer and look like extended sources, a collection of many point sources; the changes from them average out.
- **Advance sunrise and delayed sunset:** we see the Sun about **2 minutes** before it actually rises and about 2 minutes after it sets, because its light bends over the horizon.

blocks.question: Stars twinkle because of:
blocks.explanation: Changing refraction in the moving atmosphere keeps changing the apparent position and brightness of a star.
option_feedback: Stars twinkle on clear nights too.
There is no prism in the sky.

blocks.title: Why the sky is blue
blocks.body:
When a beam of light passes through a colloid such as smoke or mist, its path becomes visible because tiny particles scatter the light: the **Tyndall effect** (sunbeams entering a dense forest).

The colour of scattered light depends on the size of the particles: very fine particles scatter mainly **blue** (short wavelength) light; larger particles scatter longer wavelengths, and very large ones scatter all colours equally, so they look **white** (clouds).

- **Blue sky:** air molecules are very small, so they scatter blue light much more than red.
- **Reddish Sun at sunrise and sunset:** sunlight crosses a much thicker layer of air near the horizon, so most of the blue is scattered away and mostly red reaches us.
- **Dark sky for astronauts:** at great heights there is almost no air to scatter light.
- **Red danger signals:** red light is scattered least by fog and smoke, so it can be seen from far away.

| Everyday observation | Reason |
|---|---|
| Stars twinkle | atmospheric refraction: starlight bends by changing amounts as the air moves |
| Planets do not twinkle | a planet is an extended source; the variations from its many points cancel out |
| Sun seen about 2 minutes before sunrise and after sunset | atmospheric refraction bends sunlight over the horizon |
| Sky is blue | fine air molecules scatter blue light more than red |
| Sun looks reddish at sunrise and sunset | light travels a long path through air; most blue is scattered away |
| Sky looks dark to an astronaut | no atmosphere to scatter light high above the earth |
| Rainbow | dispersion, refraction and internal reflection of sunlight in raindrops |

blocks.question: Why does the sky appear dark to an astronaut high above the earth?
options: Space is full of black dust
There is no atmosphere to scatter sunlight
The Sun gives no blue light there
The astronaut's eyes cannot see blue
blocks.explanation: Without air to scatter light, no light reaches the eye from the sky around the Sun.

blocks.title: Lens for the eye, colour for the sky
blocks.body:
- **My**opia = **my** eyes see only near; use a **con-c-a-v-e** lens (it 'caves in' the rays).
- **Hyper**metropia = needs a **convex** (plus) lens: "hyper" goes with "plus".
- **VIBGYOR** from the base of the spectrum upwards: violet bends most.
- **Small particles, short waves (blue); big particles, all waves (white).**

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.body:
- Saying the image on the retina is erect: it is real and inverted; the brain interprets it.
- Mixing up corrections: myopia needs a concave lens, hypermetropia a convex lens.
- Writing that red bends the most in a prism: violet bends the most.
- Explaining twinkling by scattering: it is atmospheric refraction.
- Forgetting to convert cm to m when finding the power of a corrective lens.

blocks.title: Try it in class
blocks.body: Pass sunlight through a glass prism onto a white wall to show VIBGYOR, and spray water against the morning sun to make a small rainbow. Shine a torch through water with a few drops of milk: from the side the beam looks bluish, while the light coming straight through looks orange-red, just like the sky and the setting Sun.

blocks.title: Explain it in your own words
blocks.body: Explain to a friend why a myopic person needs a concave lens, and why the setting Sun looks red while the midday sky looks blue.

blocks.title: Where this leads
blocks.body:
- **Chapter 9:** lenses, focal length and power are used here to correct vision.
- **Class 12 Physics:** optical instruments, the wave nature of light and the scattering of light in detail.
- **Everyday life:** eye tests, spectacles, contact lenses, cameras and traffic signals all depend on these ideas.

blocks.title: Mastery challenge
blocks.body:
A man's near point is 50 cm. He wants to read a book held at 25 cm.

(a) What defect does he have? (b) What lens does he need, and of what power?

**Answer:** (a) Hypermetropia (or presbyopia, if it is due to age). (b) A convex lens that makes an object at 25 cm appear to be at 50 cm: $u = -25$ cm, $v = -50$ cm, $\dfrac{1}{f} = \dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1}{u} = -\dfrac{1}{50} + \dfrac{1}{25} = \dfrac{1}{50}$, so $f = 50$ cm $= 0.5$ m and $P = +2$ D.

blocks.title: Chapter summary
blocks.body:
- The eye forms a real, inverted image on the retina; the ciliary muscles change the focal length of the eye lens (accommodation). Normal near point 25 cm, far point infinity.
- Myopia is corrected by a concave lens, hypermetropia by a convex lens; presbyopia may need bifocal lenses.
- A prism deviates light and disperses white light into VIBGYOR; violet bends most and red least; a rainbow is formed by raindrops.
- Atmospheric refraction causes the twinkling of stars and the advance sunrise and delayed sunset.
- Scattering of light causes the Tyndall effect, the blue sky, the reddish Sun at sunrise and sunset, and the dark sky seen by astronauts.

blocks.title: Board exam tips
blocks.body:
- Practise ray diagrams for myopia and hypermetropia, before and after correction, and dispersion through a prism.
- For corrective lenses: myopia, f = −(far point); hypermetropia, use the lens formula with u = −25 cm and v = −(near point).
- In 'give reason' questions name the phenomenon first (refraction, dispersion, scattering), then explain.
- Learn VIBGYOR and which colour deviates most.

blocks.back: About 25 cm for a normal young adult eye.

blocks.front: Why do danger signals use red light?
blocks.back: Red light is scattered least by fog and smoke, so it can be seen from far away.
